name: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II
principal_investigator: Five PIs, each with a test series: Subrata Bhattacharjee (San Diego State University), Carlos Fernandez-Pello (UC Berkeley), Fletcher J. Miller with Indrek Wichman (San Diego State / Michigan State), Sandra L. Olson (NASA GRC), James T'ien (Case Western Reserve University)
investigators_note: Roles taken from the BASS-II Summary Report (NASA/TM-20210011385). The PSI metadata lists the same people as Co-Investigators and omits Olson.
objective: Study ignition, flame growth, flame spread and extinction limits of solid fuels burning in low-velocity forced flows in microgravity. Begin to bridge the gap between the normal-gravity NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 method, ground-based microgravity tests and actual material flammability in microgravity. Provide preliminary data to the SoFIE investigators. Examine practical, thicker fuels in typical geometries (slabs, cylinders, spherical sections). Results feed the computational models used to design fire detection and suppression systems in microgravity and on Earth.
hypothesis: Materials in microgravity, with adequate ventilation, burn as well as or better than the same material in normal gravity under otherwise identical conditions. NASA's upward-burning flammability test in normal gravity is treated as the worst case on Earth, but may not be conservative for space.
approach: Combustion tests on the ISS with real-time crew operation. Fuel samples were mounted in a small wind tunnel installed in the Microgravity Science Glovebox, with airflow up to 40 cm/s. Oxygen was lowered below 21 % by adding nitrogen. Flame appearance, growth and spread rate were measured in both opposed and concurrent flow.
fuel: cast PMMA rods, clear and black
Japan wax candle (left over from BASS-I)
geometry: films and slabs 0.1 to 5 mm thick, 1 or 2 cm wide, one- and two-sided burning; rods 6.35, 9.525 and 12.7 mm diameter (1/4, 3/8, 1/2 inch), 57 mm long; section of a 4 cm diameter sphere; flat fabric samples 1 or 2 cm wide
conditions_note: O2 range (13.6-22.2 %) is stated in the Summary Report and matches the 129 rows of the PSI experiment table. O2 was lowered by diluting the MSG working volume with nitrogen, a first on the ISS. Pressure: the report treats the working volume as 1 atm (ISS cabin); it was not varied. Ambient temperature is not stated.
flow: forced airflow from 0 to about 55 cm/s with no flow restrictor, about 35 cm/s with two restrictors; opposed, concurrent and stagnation-flow configurations; flow stepped up or down during a test to find quenching (low flow) and blowoff (high flow) limits
gravity_note: ISS; results compared with normal-gravity tests in the publications
hardware_note: Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) in the Destiny lab, with the BASS-II flow duct: a 7.6 x 7.6 x 17 cm fan-driven duct originally built for gas-jet flame studies. Hot-wire igniter operated manually by the astronaut. MSG filters capture particulates and convert CO to CO2.
sensors: color video camera (Panasonic WV-CP654) with data overlay: N2 flow, fan voltage, air velocity, radiometer signal
thermopile radiometer (Oriel 71768), uncalibrated, used for flame steadiness and oscillations
airspeed transducer (TSI 8475) for duct flow velocity
CSA-CP (Compound Specific Analyzer-Combustion Products): O2 and CO before and after each test
CDM (Carbon Dioxide Monitor): CO2 before and after each test
measured_or_computed_quantities: flame spread rate (opposed and concurrent flow)
flame shape, standoff distance and growth
quenching limit at low flow and blowoff limit at high flow
O2 consumed, CO2 and CO produced
heat release rate (by O2 consumption calorimetry)

test_summary.test_dates: February to August 2014, plus three rod tests in February 2016

key_results: PMMA rods stay flammable in microgravity down to about 13.5 % O2, well below the 15.4 % upward flame spread limit measured in normal gravity. The standard ground flammability test (NASA-STD-6001 Test 1) is therefore not conservative for space.

The flammability boundary is U-shaped: flames quench at very low flow and blow off at high flow. The most flammable condition is at weak ventilation, which the report notes is typical of spacecraft ventilation near surfaces.
Opposed-flow flame spread over black PMMA rods occurred down to 17.5 % O2 in microgravity, against 19 % in normal gravity.
Ignition is harder than sustaining a flame: ignition limits lie at higher O2 than flammability limits, and ignition delay can be almost 10 times the igniter-on time of the NASA-STD-6001 test.
The three Nomex samples did not ignite. Nomex is widely used on the ISS as a fire barrier.
A burning wax candle ejected a droplet of molten wax upstream, illustrating how melting plastics can spread fire in microgravity.
For thin PMMA films, the critical opposed-flow velocity below which the flame goes out (radiative extinction) does not depend on fuel thickness, and it rises as O2 falls.
SIBAL fabric in concurrent flow quenched at flow velocities between 1 and 5 cm/s.
Thicker fuels spread flame more slowly; two-sided burning spreads faster than one-sided. The numerical model over-predicted spread rates for thick slabs.

Combustion products: O2 burned nearly stoichiometrically to CO2, but CO-to-CO2 ratios were about ten times those of efficient combustion and CO rose sharply near the low-O2 limit. Flames were fuel rich (global equivalence ratio about 1.3). First extensive data on the toxicity of combustion products in microgravity.
Most tests released well below 100 W of heat.
space_benefits: Improved spacecraft fire safety: helps engineers select the safest materials and improve firefighting methods on future missions.
earth_benefits: The simpler flame shape in microgravity lets researchers test computer models of burning fuel, which can then be applied to wildfires, building fires, energy recovery from waste and other combustion problems.
scenario_relevance: NOT FILLED IN (to be computed from the team's ranking rules). Note: O2 range is 13.6-22.2 % at 1 atm, so it covers ISS-like atmospheres and the low-oxygen flammability limit, but not the roughly 30 % O2 at reduced pressure expected for the lunar base.
